# Poliomyelitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the central nervous system > Poliomyelitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/t40XOT)

---

## Summary

Poliomyelitis, or polio, is a disease caused by <u>poliovirus</u>, a type of human <u>Enterovirus</u>. <u>Poliovirus</u> spreads via <u>fecal-oral transmission</u>. Although the majority of <u>poliovirus</u> infections are asymptomatic, some may invade the <u>central nervous system</u>, leading to motor <u>neuron</u> <u>death</u> and irreversible <u>paralysis</u> that can cause <u>respiratory insufficiency</u> and <u>death</u>. Symptomatic poliomyelitis most commonly manifests as a <u>flu-like illness</u>. In rare cases, patients develop paralytic poliomyelitis, which manifests with <u>weakness</u>, decreased muscle tone, and <u>hyporeflexia</u>. The diagnosis is established based on <u>polymerase chain reaction</u> (<u>PCR</u>) findings of <u>poliovirus</u> <u>RNA</u> in body fluid samples (e.g., stool, oropharyngeal swab, <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u>). Poliomyelitis has been eradicated in most parts of the world as a result of <u>global</u> <u>vaccination</u> initiatives. The treatment of poliomyelitis is mainly supportive. Patients with <u>brainstem</u> or respiratory muscle involvement may require <u>intubation</u> and <u>mechanical ventilation</u>. The majority of patients with paralytic poliomyelitis do not regain their full strength after recovery. Some patients go on to develop <u>post-polio syndrome</u>, which is characterized by progressive disability and <u>muscle weakness</u> decades after the initial infection.

---

## Etiology

### Causative agent




* <u>Poliovirus</u> is an <u>RNA virus</u> in the family <u>Picornaviridae</u>, genus <u>Enterovirus</u>.

* Wild <u>poliovirus</u> type 1 causes most paralytic manifestations of poliomyelitis.  [[2]](/library/FaWgmP0)

* <u>Vaccine</u>-derived <u>poliovirus</u> type 2 (VDPV2): <u>oral polio vaccine</u> (OPV) replicates in a recently vaccinated person → viral reversion to neurovirulence → poliomyelitis in unvaccinated or <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> exposed to the recently vaccinated person [[1]](/library/xI1EUR0)

* Humans are the only hosts.





### Route of transmission [[2]](/library/FaWgmP0)




* Fecal-oral: absorption of <u>poliovirus</u> in the intestinal tract

* Droplet (rare)





### Incubation time



* 7–14 days [[3]](/library/Baaz5Q)




### <u>Risk factors for poliovirus infection</u> [[4]](/library/jdW_p40)




* Traveling to <u>endemic</u> regions

* Working with <u>polioviruses</u> specimens (e.g., laboratory workers, researchers)

* Caring for individuals likely to be infected with <u>poliovirus</u> (e.g., healthcare personnel, refugee camp workers)

* <u>Underimmunized</u> and/or <u>immunosuppressed</u> individuals [[5]](/library/rgWf9k0)

* Working or living in <u>endemic</u> regions

* In close contact with international children receiving the <u>oral poliovirus vaccine</u> (e.g., international adoptees, refugees)

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>virus</u> replicates in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> (<u>oropharynx</u> and <u>small intestine</u>) following oral ingestion → enters the bloodstream → potential invasion of the <u>gray matter</u> of the spinal cord (particularly the <u>lower motor neurons</u> of the <u>anterior horn</u>) → <u>myelitis</u>




![Spinal cord lesions](media/xde38g8rmfbcf8syrty1tyy8.jpg)

Spinal cord lesions

---

## Clinical features

Over 72% of infections with <u>poliovirus</u> are asymptomatic. Clinical infection (mostly <u>flu-like</u> symptoms) is observed in less than 24% of cases and less than 1% of infected individuals develop <u>paralysis</u>. The clinical forms of poliomyelitis are: [[3]](/library/Baaz5Q)[[6]](/library/yaadMQ)




### Poliomyelitis without <u>CNS</u> involvement (abortive poliomyelitis)




* Nonspecific symptoms: <u>gastroenteritis</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>sore throat</u>, <u>myalgia</u>, and <u>headaches</u> for 1–3 days

* Complete recovery without complications or transition to poliomyelitis with <u>CNS</u> involvement





### Poliomyelitis with <u>CNS</u> involvement




#### Nonparalytic poliomyelitis: aseptic meningitic form




* Begins several days following abortive poliomyelitis (often temporary, symptom-free interval)

* <u>Fever</u>, neck stiffness, <u>headache</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, muscle <u>pain</u>

* Neck <u>muscle weakness</u> (head drop sign: head falls back when placed in a <u>supine position</u>)

* No <u>paresis</u>





#### Paralytic poliomyelitis




* Occurs 2–3 days following the meningitic form after a brief symptom-free interval

* <u>Fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>, <u>headache</u>, <u>nausea</u>

* Severe back, neck, and muscle <u>pain</u>

* Asymmetric acute <u>flaccid paralysis</u> worsens over hours to days.

* Most commonly affects the <u>leg muscles</u>, although the arms, abdomen, trunk, thorax, and eyes may be affected

* <u>Paralysis</u> is usually more severe in <u>proximal</u> muscles than in <u>distal</u> muscles.

* Ascending <u>paralysis</u> with diaphragmatic involvement → <u>respiratory failure</u>

* Bulbar form with <u>brain stem</u> involvement (rare): damage to the cerebral or autonomic nerve centers (<u>cranial nerves</u> and <u>respiratory center</u>) → central respiratory <u>paralysis</u>

* Diminished <u>deep tendon reflexes</u>

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Hypotonia</u>

* <u>Fasciculations</u>

---

## Subtypes and variants

* Post-polio syndrome (<u>PPS</u>) [[7]](/library/FFagPm)

* Most frequent complication observed following <u>poliovirus</u> infection (up to 40% of survivors)

* Occurs decades after infection

* Manifests with progressive <u>muscle weakness</u> and <u>pain</u>, even in areas that were not affected by the initial infection

---

## Diagnosis

* Consider poliomyelitis in unvaccinated patients with nonspecific viral symptoms who: [[8]](/library/AI1R2R0)

* Live in areas with known community spread

* Have recently traveled to a region where polio has not been eradicated or OPV is still utilized

* Initial test: <u>PCR</u> of stool or oropharyngeal samples to test for <u>enterovirus</u> [[9]](/library/yI1d2R0)

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>PCR</u> of <u>CSF</u>, stool, or oropharyngeal samples to test for <u>poliovirus</u> <u>RNA</u>  [[8]](/library/AI1R2R0)

* <u>CSF</u> will show:

* High protein levels

* <u>Pleocytosis</u> with either <u>neutrophils</u> (early infection) or <u>lymphocytes</u> (late infection)

* Normal <u>glucose</u> levels

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Other viral infections: Other <u>enteroviruses</u> may also cause <u>flaccid paralysis</u>.

* <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u>: <u>Paralysis</u> is typically symmetrical in <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u>. In addition, it would not manifest with <u>CSF</u> <u>pleocytosis</u>.

* <u>Acute intermittent porphyria</u>: may also present with <u>muscle weakness</u> and <u>bulbar paralysis</u>

* <u>Spinal muscular atrophy</u>: <u>Paralysis</u> is typically symmetrical.




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

* <u>Pain</u> relief

* <u>Airway management</u> and <u>mechanical ventilation</u> if needed (e.g., <u>signs of airway compromise</u>, <u>respiratory failure</u>)

* Close monitoring of blood pressure and respiratory function

---

## Prevention

### <u>Vaccination</u> [[10]](/library/LWWwN40)[[11]](/library/6WWjm40)[[12]](/library/pWWLm40)[[13]](/library/7gW49k0)




* Available <u>vaccines</u>

* Inactivated poliovirus vaccine;  (<u>IPV</u>)

* Subcutaneous or intramuscular injection

* Can be administered individually, with other <u>vaccines</u>, or as a <u>combination vaccine</u>.

* Live-attenuated oral polio vaccine (OPV): discontinued in the US, but may be used in resource-limited countries  [[14]](/library/6tdje70)

* <u>Immunization schedule</u> [[14]](/library/6tdje70)

* <u>IPV</u> is recommended for all individuals; see the <u>ACIP immunization schedule</u> for details.

* Individuals with <u>risk factors for poliovirus infection</u> may require additional doses of <u>vaccination</u>. For more details, see: [[4]](/library/jdW_p40)[[5]](/library/rgWf9k0)[[12]](/library/pWWLm40)

* “<u>Immunization schedule by medical indication</u>”

* “<u>Vaccines before travel</u>”
